title: RiSE: Residual Subspace Expert for Generalizable Text-Centric Image Forgery Localization

paper.title: RiSE: R es i dual S ubspace E xpert for Generalizable Text-Centric Image Forgery Localization
paper.abstract:
Abstract As AI-assisted image editing becomes increasingly prevalent, Text-Centric Image Forgery Localization (TFL) is essential for protecting trust in financial and legal records. However, we observe that existing TFL detectors predominantly rely on Full-Parameter Fine-Tuning (FPFT) and fail to generalize to unseen forgery types because FPFT can induce low-rank feature collapse and overfit training artifacts. Meanwhile, prior detectors capture diverse forgery traces with a single unified representation, making subtle traces entangled and difficult to learn. To address these challenges, we propose RiSE , a Residual Subspace Expert model that preserves pre-trained priors by freezing principal SVD components and adapting only the residual subspaces with a ViT-only segmentor to avoid feature collapse. RiSE introduces forgery-aware residual experts, where each expert is trained independently on a training subset with a particular forgery type, and we show that cross-domain localization performance improves consistently as more experts are added. At inference, we introduce Latent Perturbation Confidence (LPC), which selects the most confident expert by analytically computing the latent-perturbed output. LPC enables efficient confidence estimation with a single forward pass, avoiding repeated forward passes on perturbed samples and improving expert selection.
By training on synthetic forgery data, RiSE with 1 expert outperforms prior methods on real-world forgery images by 20.4% while reducing training steps by 10 × 10\times . Scaling the number of experts to 9 yields a 35.8% gain. RiSE remains effective with DCT feature, even when the majority of the parameters is frozen with RGB-only pretraining. sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Text-Centric Image Forgery Localization (TFL) aims to identify manipulated regions in scanned or captured text-centric images. This problem is increasingly important because modern AI-assisted editing tools allow ordinary users to alter document and scene-text images with little expertise ( Wong et al., 2025b ; Wong et al., 2025a ; Wong et al., 2026b ) , threatening trust in images used for financial verification, legal review, and identity authentication. Although recent TFL methods have improved accuracy by combining RGB, frequency ( Qu et al., 2023 ) , and multi-scale cues ( Dong et al., 2024 ) , their performance still drops sharply under cross-domain evaluation, where unseen forgery patterns and acquisition artifacts differ from the training distribution ( Du et al., 2025 ; Gushchin and others, 2026 ) . We argue that this failure is not merely a data scarcity issue. Unlike semantic segmentation, TFL depends on weak, non-semantic forensic traces whose statistics vary sharply across editing pipelines, recompression settings, and capture conditions. As a result, many existing TFL detectors ( Qu et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Wong et al., 2025c ) rely on Full-Parameter Fine-Tuning (FPFT) and end up specializing to the limited forgery patterns seen during training. Their penultimate features become highly low-rank, as shown in Fig. 1 , indicating representation collapse that harms cross-domain generalization. This observation points to a different formulation of TFL: the central challenge is to control where task-specific adaptation happens. Recent work on residual subspace adaptation ( Yan et al., 2025 ) shows that transferable priors from Vision Foundation Models (VFMs), typically built on the Vision Transformer ( Dosovitskiy et al., 2021 ) (ViT) architecture (e.g., CLIP ( Radford et al., 2021 ) , DINOv2 ( Oquab et al., 2024 ) , and DINOv3 ( Siméoni et al., 2025 ) ), can be preserved by freezing the dominant SVD components of ViT linear layers and fine-tuning only residual subspaces. This prior-preserving adaptation avoids representation collapse and improves performance in AI-generated image detection ( Yan et al., 2025 ) . However, bringing this idea to TFL requires more than inserting residual adaptation into an off-the-shelf segmentor. In TFL, the task-specific decoders and fusion modules can become a second adaptation pathway, allowing the model to memorize dataset-specific compression, synthesis, or capture artifacts outside the pre-trained backbone. At the same time, learning all forgery types in a single shared residual space entangles heterogeneous traces, causing subtle manipulation cues to be overwhelmed by dominant but less transferable patterns. This leads to two questions: (1) Can TFL be reformulated as a prior-preserving localization problem, with minimal trainable modules beyond the ViT so that adaptation remains constrained and transferable? (2) Can the limited trainable capacity be expertized, so that different residual subspaces specialize to complementary forgery cues and generalize better under domain shift? To answer these questions, we propose RiSE , a R es i dual S ubspace E xpert model for TFL built on a ViT-only segmenter. We instantiate RiSE on EoMT ( Kerssies et al., 2025 ) , which turns a ViT into a segmenter using only query embeddings and a lightweight mask module, thereby minimizing additional adaptation pathways beyond the backbone. On top of this architecture, RiSE divides the training set into non-overlapping subsets with a particular forgery type and trains one residual expert on each subset independently. All experts share the dominant principal subspaces of the VFM backbone, while each expert learns only a tiny residual subspace tailored to a more homogeneous forgery regime. We show that this offline image-level routing is more stable than learnable routing ( Shazeer et al., 2017 ) , and that scaling the number of experts consistently improves cross-domain performance as shown in Fig. 2 while parameter growth remains sublinear because the principal components are shared among experts. To select the final prediction among experts, we further propose Latent Perturbation Confidence (LPC), which addresses the limitation that existing confidence metrics ( Hendrycks and Gimpel, 2017 ; Borges et al., 2024 ) often become unreliable when forged regions are small. LPC estimates the expected latent-perturbed output analytically and favors experts whose forged predictions remain stable under perturbations. As a result, LPC enables single-pass confidence estimation, avoiding repeated forward passes on perturbed samples and improving expert selection for more accurate localization. Trained on DocTamper ( Qu et al., 2023 ) synthetic forgery data, a single RiSE expert generalizes effectively to real-world forgery images, achieving a substantial 20.4% performance improvement while reducing training steps by 10 × 10\times compared with existing TFL methods. Scaling to 9 experts further boosts the performance gain to 35.8%. Our contributions are fourfold: • We identify uncontrolled task-specific adaptation as a key cause of poor cross-domain TFL, show that FPFT induces low-rank feature collapse, and reformulate TFL as a prior-preserving localization problem with a ViT-only residual adaptation architecture. • We introduce residual subspace experts for TFL, each optimized on a training subset with a specific forgery type, so that different residual subspaces specialize to complementary forgery cues and improve cross-domain localization as more experts are added while keeping parameter growth sublinear. • We develop a plug-and-play confidence estimator, LPC, that analytically computes expected latent-perturbed outputs to measure expert confidence effectively and efficiently. • Extensive experiments demonstrate that RiSE consistently improves cross-domain localization performance by 35.8% across 4 test sets.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: General image forgery localization increasingly focuses on robust trace modeling across manipulation types. Representative methods such as MVSS-Net ( Chen et al., 2021 ) and PSCC-Net ( Liu et al., 2022 ) use multi-scale cues, CAT-Net ( Kwon et al., 2022 ) exploits JPEG DCT statistics, and later work including IFOSN ( Wu et al., 2022 ) , TruFor ( Guillaro et al., 2023 ) , FOCAL ( Wu et al., 2025 ) , and Mesorch ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) improves generalization through modeling Online Social Networks (OSN) transmission, noise fingerprint, contrastive feature, and designing CNN–Transformer structure. Nevertheless, general image forgery detectors often struggle on text-centric images because forged regions can blend into the uniform backgrounds and structured text layouts. Text-centric image forgery localization has progressed from early benchmarking to DCT-aware and robustness-oriented detectors ( Wong et al., 2026a ) . DTD ( Qu et al., 2023 ) introduced the DocTamper benchmarking and showed that DCT perception with multi-scale decoding can effectively localize tampered regions. FFDN ( Chen et al., 2024 ) and ADCD-Net ( Wong et al., 2025c ) further improved localization through RGB–DCT fusion, with ADCD-Net explicitly addressing DCT misalignment and text-background disparity. TIFDM ( Dong et al., 2024 ) strengthens trace enhancement and multi-scale aggregation under degradations, CAFTB ( Song et al., 2025 ) combines spatial and noise-domain cues with cross-attention fusion, and DITL 2 \text{DITL}^{2} improves performance through learning from both general and text-centric image forgeries ( Li et al., 2025 ) . However, most existing TFL detectors rely on FPFT, which overfits training forgery patterns and induces low-rank feature collapse, harming cross-domain generalization. In contrast, RiSE preserves transferable priors via residual subspace adaptation and uses forgery-aware residual experts for stronger specialization and generalization.

sections.heading: Motivation.
sections.text: Recent TFL methods such as DTD ( Qu et al., 2023 ) , FFDN ( Chen et al., 2024 ) , and ADCD-Net ( Wong et al., 2025c ) rely on FPFT. As shown in Fig. 1 , these models produce strongly low-rank features, overfit to training forgery traces, and perform worse on cross-domain data ( Du et al., 2025 ) . Motivated by residual subspace adaptation ( Yan et al., 2025 ) , we use a ViT-only segmenter ( Kerssies et al., 2025 ) to keep the architecture minimal and preserve transferable VFM priors. RiSE maintains an effective rank that is roughly 4.7 − 37.3 × 4.7-37.3\times higher than these prior methods across the 8 datasets, suggesting that residual subspace adaptation better preserves transferable knowledge and avoids feature collapse. The effective rank computation is detailed in Appendix C . Our second motivation is the scaling behavior of residual experts. For TFL, we argue that modeling diverse forgery patterns and image context with a single space could lead to entangled and noisy representations ( Tu et al., 2026 ) . Therefore, we propose to split the training data into subsets with a particular forgery type and train a residual expert on each subset independently. Adding residual experts consistently improves training optimization in Fig. 2 (a), as well as enhancing cross-domain localization in Fig. 2 (b). For RiSE with multiple experts, we report the oracle performance, which assumes access to the ground-truth mask to choose the best expert for each sample and therefore serves as an upper bound on expert selection.

As shown in Fig. 3 (b), an expert consists of three modules: a ViT-based VFM backbone, an optional DCT module, and a mask module. sections.heading: DCT module.
sections.text: As demonstrated in prior TFL studies ( Chen et al., 2024 ; Wong et al., 2025c ) , DCT traces improve robustness to recompression. However, such traces can also become a shortcut, causing the model to over-rely on DCT cues instead of RGB evidence. RiSE encodes the DCT coefficients 𝐗 dct \mathbf{X}_{\mathrm{dct}} and quantization table 𝐗 qt \mathbf{X}_{\mathrm{qt}} with the DCT encoder ϕ dct \phi_{\mathrm{dct}} in ( Qu et al., 2023 ) , and obtains DCT features 𝐙 dct = ϕ dct ​ ( 𝐗 dct , 𝐗 qt ) \mathbf{Z}_{\mathrm{dct}}=\phi_{\mathrm{dct}}(\mathbf{X}_{\mathrm{dct}},\mathbf{X}_{\mathrm{qt}}) . The DCT features then conditionally fuse with the RGB features using an image-level Bernoulli gate, 𝐙 fuse = 𝐙 rgb + g ​ 𝐙 dct \mathbf{Z}_{\mathrm{fuse}}=\mathbf{Z}_{\mathrm{rgb}}+g\,\mathbf{Z}_{\mathrm{dct}} with g ∼ Bernoulli ⁡ ( p g ) g\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p_{g}) , where p g = 0.5 p_{g}=0.5 is the default DCT fusion probability during training, and p g = 1.0 p_{g}=1.0 at inference. This random gate balances DCT and RGB learning by randomly dropping DCT traces during training, reducing reliance on DCT shortcuts. Unlike ADCD-Net ( Wong et al., 2025c ) , which uses a learnable DCT fusion score, our design does not assume DCT-grid alignment and avoids extra computation from alignment-breaking augmentations and score-learning modules. We observe that RiSE remains robust to such auxiliary cues despite freezing the principal components of an RGB-pretrained VFM, and future work could extend this fusion to noise prints ( Guillaro et al., 2023 ) , boundary traces ( Liu et al., 2024 ) , or edit traces ( Wu et al., 2026 ) .

sections.heading: 3.2 RiSE Inference
sections.text: As suggested by the expert-scaling trend in Fig. 2 (b), adding residual experts improves cross-domain oracle F1. sections.heading: MSP.
sections.text: As a simple baseline, we compute the average Maximum Softmax Probability (MSP) across all pixels ( Hendrycks and Gimpel, 2017 ) , MSP ⁡ ( 𝐩 ^ ) = 1 N pix ​ ∑ n = 1 N pix max ⁡ { 𝐩 ^ ​ ( n ) , 1 − 𝐩 ^ ​ ( n ) } \mathrm{MSP}(\hat{\mathbf{p}})=\frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{pix}}}\sum_{n=1}^{N_{\mathrm{pix}}}\max\{\hat{\mathbf{p}}(n),\,1-\hat{\mathbf{p}}(n)\} . However, MSP can be dominated by the easy pristine pixels and underestimate the influence of tiny tampered regions. This motivates the usage of SDC, which focuses on the foreground confidence.

sections.heading: SDC.
sections.text: To address the extreme class imbalance, Soft Dice Confidence (SDC) ( Borges et al., 2024 ) does not consider true negative predictions and therefore ignores the huge easy pristine area: SDC ⁡ ( 𝐩 ^ ) = 2 ​ 𝐩 ^ ⊤ ​ 𝐲 ^ / ( ‖ 𝐩 ^ ‖ 1 + ‖ 𝐲 ^ ‖ 1 ) \mathrm{SDC}(\hat{\mathbf{p}})=2\hat{\mathbf{p}}^{\top}\hat{\mathbf{y}}/(\|\hat{\mathbf{p}}\|_{1}+\|\hat{\mathbf{y}}\|_{1}) , where 𝐲 ^ = 𝟙 [ 𝐩 ^ > τ ] ∈ { 0 , 1 } N pix \hat{\mathbf{y}}=\mathds{1}[\hat{\mathbf{p}}>\tau]\in\{0,1\}^{N_{\mathrm{pix}}} , in which τ \tau is the binarization threshold. SDC favors experts that consistently produce high probabilities for the forged area. Although SDC improves over MSP, it still lags behind oracle performance.

sections.heading: LPC.
sections.text: Our proposed LPC builds on SDC with a simple intuition: an expert should be trusted when its confidences remain stable under perturbed inputs. We therefore compute SDC on the prediction obtained by averaging over multiple Test-Time Augmentations (TTA), and Appendix D provides a justification for why TTA averaging stabilizes SDC. Formally, let T ⁡ ( ⋅ ) T(\cdot) be an augmentation (e.g. flipping, rotation, noise), and the TTA-averaged prediction be 𝐩 ¯ = 1 M ​ ∑ m = 1 M T m − 1 ​ ( E ⁡ ( T m ​ ( 𝐗 ) ) ) \bar{\mathbf{p}}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}T_{m}^{-1}\!\left(E(T_{m}(\mathbf{X}))\right) , where T m − 1 T_{m}^{-1} maps the prediction back to the original coordinates, and for non-spatial perturbations such as additive Gaussian noise, T m − 1 T_{m}^{-1} is the identity map. We then compute SDC on 𝐩 ¯ \bar{\mathbf{p}} to obtain the TTA-SDC score. However, this input-space TTA is computationally expensive, yielding M M forward passes per image. To avoid the cost of TTA, we propose to apply perturbations directly to the latent space, that is the VFM output feature 𝐙 vfm \mathbf{Z}_{\mathrm{vfm}} : LPC ⁡ ( 𝐙 vfm ) = SDC ⁡ ( 𝐩 ¯ lat ) , 𝐩 ¯ lat = 1 M ​ ∑ m = 1 M T m − 1 ​ ( ϕ mask ​ ( 𝐐 vfm , T m ​ ( 𝐙 vfm ) ) ) , \mathrm{LPC}(\mathbf{Z}_{\mathrm{vfm}})=\mathrm{SDC}\bigl(\bar{\mathbf{p}}_{\mathrm{lat}}\bigr),\qquad\bar{\mathbf{p}}_{\mathrm{lat}}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}T_{m}^{-1}\!\left(\phi_{\mathrm{mask}}\bigl(\mathbf{Q}_{\mathrm{vfm}},T_{m}(\mathbf{Z}_{\mathrm{vfm}})\bigr)\right), where ϕ mask \phi_{\mathrm{mask}} is the mask module. Compared with image-space TTA, LPC avoids repeated VFM forwards by perturbing only the latent features. For Gaussian latent perturbations, T m ​ ( 𝐙 vfm ) = 𝐙 vfm + ϵ m , ϵ m ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝟎 , σ 2 ​ I ) . T_{m}(\mathbf{Z}_{\mathrm{vfm}})=\mathbf{Z}_{\mathrm{vfm}}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{m},\qquad\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{m}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\sigma^{2}I). The averaged output can then be written as the expected latent-perturbed output: 𝐩 ¯ lat = 𝔼 ϵ ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝟎 , σ 2 ​ I ) ​ [ ϕ mask ​ ( 𝐐 vfm , 𝐙 vfm + ϵ ) ] . \bar{\mathbf{p}}_{\mathrm{lat}}=\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\sigma^{2}I)}\bigl[\phi_{\mathrm{mask}}(\mathbf{Q}_{\mathrm{vfm}},\mathbf{Z}_{\mathrm{vfm}}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon})\bigr]. We find that this expectation admits an analytic approximation, without explicitly sampling the M M perturbations. Concretely, we propagate the mean and variance through the mask module using Assumed Density Filtering (ADF) ( Gast and Roth, 2018 ) and details are provided in Appendix E . As a result, LPC requires only a single forward pass through both the VFM and the mask module.

sections.heading: Dataset.
sections.text: We adapt the Doc Protocol in ForensicHub ( Du et al., 2025 ) for the main experiments. All models are trained only on the DocTamper training split ( Qu et al., 2023 ) and are evaluated on seven test sets: three in-domain DocTamper test sets, FCD , SCD , and Test , and four cross-domain test sets, T-SROIE ( Wang et al., 2022b ) , OSTF ( Qu et al., 2025 ) , TPIC-13 ( Wang et al., 2022a ) , and RTM ( Luo et al., 2025 ) . Details of the datasets are provided in Appendix Table 5 .

sections.heading: Competitors.
sections.text: We compare RiSE with six general image forgery localization methods: MVSS-Net ( Chen et al., 2021 ) , PSCC-Net ( Liu et al., 2022 ) , CAT-Net ( Kwon et al., 2022 ) , TruFor ( Guillaro et al., 2023 ) , IML-ViT ( Ma et al., 2023 ) , and Mesorch ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) , as well as five recent TFL methods: DTD ( Qu et al., 2023 ) , FFDN ( Chen et al., 2024 ) , CAFTB ( Song et al., 2025 ) , TIFDM ( Dong et al., 2024 ) , and ADCD-Net ( Wong et al., 2025c ) .

sections.heading: Implementation.
sections.text: RiSE uses DINOv3 ViT-L/16 ( Siméoni et al., 2025 ) as the VFM backbone, with L 1 = 10 L_{1}=10 , L 2 = 10 L_{2}=10 , and L 3 = 4 L_{3}=4 blocks. The RiSE design choices are detailed in the ablation study in Table 4.2 . We train RiSE for 10,000 steps with the AdamW optimizer, using a learning rate of 3 ​ e − 4 3e-4 decayed to 1 ​ e − 5 1e-5 via cosine annealing, and a batch size of 16. Detailed training and inference efficiency are provided in Appendix Table 16 .

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We presented RiSE, a residual subspace expert model for text-centric image forgery localization. Motivated by the observation that FPFT causes low-rank feature collapse and poor cross-domain generalization, RiSE freezes the dominant VFM subspace, adapts only a small residual component, and scales capacity through independently trained forgery-aware experts. We also introduced LPC, a confidence estimator that selects experts by measuring prediction stability under latent perturbations via a single-pass approximation. Experiments show that RiSE consistently improves cross-domain localization as the number of experts increases. In particular, relative to ADCD-Net, RiSE-1 improves AvgC by 20.4%, and scaling to RiSE-9 increases the gain to 35.8%. RiSE-9-DCT obtains an in-domain average F1 of 0.767 0.767 , a cross-domain average F1 of 0.616 0.616 , and an overall average F1 of 0.681 0.681 . These results suggest that preserving transferable VFM priors while scaling expertized residual capacity is a promising direction for robust and efficient TFL.

sections.heading: Appendix B Expert Assignment
sections.text: RiSE uses different training-set partitions for different numbers of experts. RiSE-1 uses the entire training set as a single subset. RiSE-3 uses the forgery synthesis type as the subset label, which splits the training set into three subsets corresponding to copy-move (CM), splicing (SP), and generation (GE). RiSE-9 uses a finer expert-assignment label d i d_{i} for each training sample by combining two attributes, the forgery synthesis type s i s_{i} and the feature cluster index k i k_{i} . The forgery synthesis type is provided directly by the DocTamper metadata (see https://github.com/qcf-568/DocTamper ). Each training sample belongs to one of the three synthesis categories CM, SP, or GE. The training set contains 35,000 CM samples, 45,000 SP samples, and 40,000 GE samples. We use this label as the first-level partition because these three manipulation sources exhibit different forensic traces and therefore benefit from separate expert specialization. The feature cluster index is obtained from the single output query embedding of a trained RiSE-1 model. Specifically, RiSE sets N q = 1 N_{q}=1 , so for each training image the model produces one output query embedding, which we denote by 𝐪 i ∈ ℝ d \mathbf{q}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} . We use this single query embedding rather than spatially pooled dense features because pooled dense tokens can mix authentic and tampered regions, especially when the forged area is small, which entangles real and fake evidence in a single representation. In contrast, the output query embedding is optimized by the localization objective to summarize tampering-relevant evidence at the image level, making it a cleaner feature for clustering. For each forgery type s s , let 𝒬 s = { 𝐪 i ∣ s i = s } \mathcal{Q}_{s}=\{\mathbf{q}_{i}\mid s_{i}=s\} . We first run standard K-means with N c N_{c} clusters on 𝒬 s \mathcal{Q}_{s} to obtain initial cluster centers { 𝝁 s , k } k = 1 N c \{\boldsymbol{\mu}_{s,k}\}_{k=1}^{N_{c}} . To prevent a few clusters from dominating the training set, we then rebalance the assignments with a balanced-clustering step that approximately solves min { k i } ∑ i : s i = s ∥ 𝐪 i − 𝝁 s , k i ∥ 2 2 s.t. | { i : s i = s , k i = k } | ∈ { ⌊ | 𝒬 s | N c ⌋ , ⌈ | 𝒬 s | N c ⌉ } , ∀ k . \min_{\{k_{i}\}}\;\sum_{i:s_{i}=s}\lVert\mathbf{q}_{i}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{s,k_{i}}\rVert_{2}^{2}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\bigl|\{i:s_{i}=s,\,k_{i}=k\}\bigr|\in\left\{\left\lfloor\frac{|\mathcal{Q}_{s}|}{N_{c}}\right\rfloor,\left\lceil\frac{|\mathcal{Q}_{s}|}{N_{c}}\right\rceil\right\},\ \forall k. In practice, we implement this balancing with a greedy reassignment procedure. Samples are sorted by their nearest-center distance, and each sample is assigned to the closest cluster whose capacity has not yet been filled. If all preferred clusters are already full, the sample is assigned to the currently smallest cluster. This produces nearly equal cluster sizes within each forgery type while staying close to the original K-means solution. After obtaining both attributes, we define the final expert-assignment label as d i = ( s i − 1 ) ​ N c + k i , d_{i}=(s_{i}-1)N_{c}+k_{i}, which yields N e = N s ​ N c N_{e}=N_{s}N_{c} non-overlapping expert assignments.

sections.heading: Appendix C Effective Rank Computation
sections.text: We compute effective rank from the empirical PCA spectrum of the saved penultimate features of DTD, FFDN, ADCD-Net and our RiSE-1 with 100 samples per dataset. For each image, we spatially average the penultimate feature map into a single feature vector, then stack the resulting vectors into a feature matrix 𝐅 ∈ ℝ 100 × d \mathbf{F}\in\mathbb{R}^{100\times d} , where d d is the feature dimension. After centering 𝐅 \mathbf{F} , we compute singular values { α a } \{\alpha_{a}\} and convert them into normalized spectral weights ρ a = η a ∑ b η b , η a = α a 2 100 − 1 . \rho_{a}=\frac{\eta_{a}}{\sum_{b}\eta_{b}},\qquad\eta_{a}=\frac{\alpha_{a}^{2}}{100-1}. Following the entropy-based definition used in low-rank analysis, the effective rank is erank ( 𝐅 ) = exp ( − ∑ a ρ a log ρ a ) . \mathrm{erank}(\mathbf{F})=\exp\left(-\sum_{a}\rho_{a}\log\rho_{a}\right). Intuitively, the effective rank measures how many principal directions are effectively used by the representation. If almost all variance is concentrated in one or two directions, the effective rank is close to 1 1 , such as DTD, FFDN, ADCD-Net in Fig. 1 . If variance is distributed more evenly across many directions, the effective rank increases, such as RiSE-1 in Fig. 1 .

sections.heading: Appendix E Moment Propagation in the Mask Module
sections.text: This section gives the implementation details of the proposed Analytic Gaussian Propagation (AGP) used by the Latent Perturbation Confidence (LPC). We first summarize the deterministic forward pass of the mask module with the PyTorch-style Pseudocode 1 , then give the Assumed Density Filtering (ADF) rules for propagating the mean and variance under latent Gaussian perturbations.

sections.heading: Mask module forward.
sections.text: For an image, the VFM produces output queries 𝐐 vfm ∈ ℝ N q × d \mathbf{Q}_{\mathrm{vfm}}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{q}\times d} and dense tokens 𝐙 vfm ∈ ℝ H p ​ W p × d \mathbf{Z}_{\mathrm{vfm}}\in\mathbb{R}^{H_{p}W_{p}\times d} . Since RiSE uses a single query, the class head ϕ cls \phi_{\mathrm{cls}} can be ignored. The mask head maps them into mask-space features 𝐐 mask = ϕ mlp ​ ( 𝐐 vfm ) \mathbf{Q}_{\mathrm{mask}}=\phi_{\mathrm{mlp}}(\mathbf{Q}_{\mathrm{vfm}}) and 𝐙 mask = ϕ up ​ ( 𝐙 vfm ) \mathbf{Z}_{\mathrm{mask}}=\phi_{\mathrm{up}}(\mathbf{Z}_{\mathrm{vfm}}) , where ϕ mlp \phi_{\mathrm{mlp}} is a three-layer MLP with GELU activations and ϕ up \phi_{\mathrm{up}} is a stack of blocks consisting of transposed-convolution, GELU, depth-wise convolution, and LayerNorm2d. The transformed query embedding and dense feature map are combined by the matching operation torch.einsum("bqc,bchw->bqhw", Q_mask, Z_mask) , followed by the sigmoid. sections.heading: Appendix G Efficiency
sections.text: Table 16 reports the measured efficiency of the RiSE variants on 4 4 NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPUs.

sections.heading: Parameter count.
sections.text: Relative to RiSE-1, scaling to RiSE-3 and RiSE-9 increases the total parameter count by only 1.003 × 1.003\times and 1.011 × 1.011\times , while the trainable parameter count increases by 1.07 × 1.07\times and 1.29 × 1.29\times . This mild growth is consistent with the RiSE design, where the dominant VFM parameters and the mask module are shared, and each additional expert contributes only a small residual subspace.

sections.heading: Training time.
sections.text: We adopt an MoE-style implementation so that multiple RiSE experts are optimized within one unified training process rather than launched as fully separate training jobs. Unlike conventional MoE, RiSE does not introduce a learnable router during training. Instead, the routing path is deterministically given by the expert-assignment label for each sample described in Section B . This fixed-routing implementation keeps the experts specialized on their assigned training subsets while reducing the overhead compared with training each expert completely in isolation. The main extra cost appears during training because more experts still require more forward and optimization runs, increasing training time by 2.66 × 2.66\times for RiSE-3 and 7.08 × 7.08\times for RiSE-9 relative to RiSE-1. Nevertheless, RiSE remains efficient in the training phase because each expert is trained for only 10k steps, which is 10 × 10\times fewer than the 100 100 k steps commonly used by existing TFL detectors [ Du et al., 2025 ] . On the same 4 4 RTX 4090 GPUs, the strong TFL baseline ADCD-Net requires approximately 27 27 training hours, so even RiSE-9 is still about 3.4 × 3.4\times faster to train.

sections.text: For inference, we convert throughput to per-sample latency in seconds. Since the experts can be executed in parallel, inference time does not grow linearly with the number of experts. sections.heading: Server-side forensic analysis.
sections.text: Inference cost increases with expert count, but our target TFL deployment is server-side forensic analysis rather than real-time edge inference. This setting can use powerful GPU resources and does not require real-time processing. It is consistent with practical document-verification scenarios such as online banking and Know Your Customer (KYC), where images are submitted for automated forensic analysis. Recent work also frames ID-document forgery detection and localization in online authentication settings [ Korshunov et al., 2025 ] .

sections.heading: Dynamic early exit.
sections.text: A dynamic early-exit mechanism is a natural extension. EoMT could decode segmentation predictions from intermediate ViT blocks with homogeneous feature shapes, allowing LPC-based confidence evaluation at intermediate layers for early termination, analogous to confident layer decoding in LLMs [ Zhang et al., 2026 ] . Developing and evaluating such a strategy is beyond the scope of this paper, and we leave it for future work.

sections.heading: Expert merging.
sections.text: Merging expert models into a unified model is another promising direction. Existing work on task arithmetic, common and task-specific subspaces, and SVD-based alignment for LoRA merging could provide practical starting points [ Ilharco et al., 2023 , Marczak et al., 2025 , Stoica et al., 2025 ] . Adapting these methods to RiSE’s residual subspace experts and evaluating the resulting accuracy–efficiency trade-off remain future work.

sections.heading: Appendix I Limitation
sections.text: RiSE has several limitations. First, scaling the number of residual experts improves cross-domain F1 but requires evaluating all experts at inference. In the single-GPU measurement, RiSE-9 uses 21,691 MiB of memory and takes 0.3571 seconds per 512 × 512 512\times 512 image; this limits its use in resource-constrained settings. Early-exit expert pruning and residual-expert merging are promising directions for reducing this cost, but we have not evaluated them here. Second, LPC still leaves a gap to the oracle selector, and exact top-1 routing agreement is modest for RiSE-9. Third, RTM remains difficult because the source training data provide limited coverage of manual erasure, physical edits, and other handcrafted manipulations. Our added corruption experiments cover JPEG recompression and resizing; dedicated print-and-scan robustness evaluation remains future work.

sections.heading: Appendix J Broader Impacts
sections.text: The proliferation of document forgery poses significant risks to information integrity, financial security, and legal processes. By improving the robustness of document forgery detection across diverse manipulation types and domains, our work contributes to safeguarding against these threats. However, it is important to consider potential misuse of such detection technologies, such as infringing on privacy or being used for surveillance. We advocate for responsible deployment of forgery detection systems with appropriate safeguards to balance security benefits with ethical considerations.

sections.heading: NeurIPS Paper Checklist
sections.text: 1. Claims Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper’s contributions and scope? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The claims match theoretical and experimental results. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper. • The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. A [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers. • The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings. • It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper. 2. Limitations Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The paper includes a dedicated section discussing the limitations of the proposed approach. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper. • The authors are encouraged to create a separate “Limitations” section in their paper. • The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be. • The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on a few datasets or with a few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated. • The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, a facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or a speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon. • The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size. • If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness. • While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, a worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that aren’t acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations. 3. Theory assumptions and proofs Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and a complete (and correct) proof? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The paper provides all necessary assumptions and complete proofs for the theoretical results. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results. • All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and cross-referenced. • All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems. • The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide a short proof sketch to provide intuition. • Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material. • Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced. 4. Experimental result reproducibility Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The paper provides all necessary details for reproducing the main experimental results, including dataset descriptions, model architectures, and training procedures. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • If the paper includes experiments, a [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not. • If the contribution is a dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable. • Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is a novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is a specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to a hosted model (e.g., in the case of a large language model), releasing of a model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed. • While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example (a) If the contribution is primarily a new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm. (b) If the contribution is primarily a new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully. (c) If the contribution is a new model (e.g., a large language model), then there should either be a way to access this model for reproducing the results or a way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset). (d) We recognize that reproducibility may be tricky in some cases, in which case authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility. In the case of closed-source models, it may be that access to the model is limited in some way (e.g., to registered users), but it should be possible for other researchers to have some path to reproducing or verifying the results. 5. Open access to data and code Question: Does the paper provide open access to the data and code, with sufficient instructions to faithfully reproduce the main experimental results, as described in supplemental material? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The paper provides all necessary instructions and resources to reproduce the main experimental results, including access to code and model checkpoints. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that paper does not include experiments requiring code. • Please see the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines ( https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy ) for more details. • While we encourage the release of code and data, we understand that this might not be possible, so [No] is an acceptable answer. Papers cannot be rejected simply for not including code, unless this is central to the contribution (e.g., for a new open-source benchmark). • The instructions should contain the exact command and environment needed to run to reproduce the results. See the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines ( https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy ) for more details. • The authors should provide instructions on data access and preparation, including how to access the raw data, preprocessed data, intermediate data, and generated data, etc. • The authors should provide scripts to reproduce all experimental results for the new proposed method and baselines. If only a subset of experiments are reproducible, they should state which ones are omitted from the script and why. • At submission time, to preserve anonymity, the authors should release anonymized versions (if applicable). • Providing as much information as possible in supplemental material (appended to the paper) is recommended, but including URLs to data and code is permitted. 6. Experimental setting/details Question: Does the paper specify all the training and test details (e.g., data splits, hyperparameters, how they were chosen, type of optimizer) necessary to understand the results? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The paper provides all necessary details for reproducing the main experimental results, including dataset descriptions, model architectures, and training procedures. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • The experimental setting should be presented in the core of the paper to a level of detail that is necessary to appreciate the results and make sense of them. • The full details can be provided either with the code, in appendix, or as supplemental material. 7. Experiment statistical significance Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly defined or other appropriate information about the statistical significance of the experiments? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The paper evaluates the proposed method on large-scale test sets. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • The authors should answer [Yes] if the results are accompanied by error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, at least for the experiments that support the main claims of the paper. • The factors of variability that the error bars are capturing should be clearly stated (for example, train/test split, initialization, random drawing of some parameter, or overall run with given experimental conditions). • The method for calculating the error bars should be explained (closed form formula, call to a library function, bootstrap, etc.) • The assumptions made should be given (e.g., Normally distributed errors). • It should be clear whether the error bar is the standard deviation or the standard error of the mean. • It is OK to report 1-sigma error bars, but one should state it. The authors should preferably report a 2-sigma error bar than state that they have a 96% CI, if the hypothesis of Normality of errors is not verified. • For asymmetric distributions, the authors should be careful not to show in tables or figures symmetric error bars that would yield results that are out of range (e.g., negative error rates). • If error bars are reported in tables or plots, the authors should explain in the text how they were calculated and reference the corresponding figures or tables in the text. 8. Experiments compute resources Question: For each experiment, does the paper provide sufficient information on the computer resources (type of compute workers, memory, time of execution) needed to reproduce the experiments? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The paper provides the hardware specifications and computational requirements for reproducing the experiments. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • The paper should indicate the type of compute workers CPU or GPU, internal cluster, or cloud provider, including relevant memory and storage. • The paper should provide the amount of compute required for each of the individual experimental runs as well as estimate the total compute. • The paper should disclose whether the full research project required more compute than the experiments reported in the paper (e.g., preliminary or failed experiments that didn’t make it into the paper). 9. Code of ethics Question: Does the research conducted in the paper conform, in every respect, with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics https://neurips.cc/public/EthicsGuidelines ? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The research conducted in the paper adheres to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the authors have not reviewed the NeurIPS Code of Ethics. • If the authors answer [No] , they should explain the special circumstances that require a deviation from the Code of Ethics. • The authors should make sure to preserve anonymity (e.g., if there is a special consideration due to laws or regulations in their jurisdiction). 10. Broader impacts Question: Does the paper discuss both potential positive societal impacts and negative societal impacts of the work performed? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The paper discusses both potential positive and negative societal impacts of the work performed. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that there is no societal impact of the work performed. • If the authors answer [N/A] or [No] , they should explain why their work has no societal impact or why the paper does not address societal impact. • Examples of negative societal impacts include potential malicious or unintended uses (e.g., disinformation, generating fake profiles, surveillance), fairness considerations (e.g., deployment of technologies that could make decisions that unfairly impact specific groups), privacy considerations, and security considerations. • The conference expects that many papers will be foundational research and not tied to particular applications, let alone deployments. However, if there is a direct path to any negative applications, the authors should point it out. For example, it is legitimate to point out that an improvement in the quality of generative models could be used to generate Deepfakes for disinformation. On the other hand, it is not needed to point out that a generic algorithm for optimizing neural networks could enable people to train models that generate Deepfakes faster. • The authors should consider possible harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended and functioning correctly, harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended but gives incorrect results, and harms following from (intentional or unintentional) misuse of the technology. • If there are negative societal impacts, the authors could also discuss possible mitigation strategies (e.g., gated release of models, providing defenses in addition to attacks, mechanisms for monitoring misuse, mechanisms to monitor how a system learns from feedback over time, improving the efficiency and accessibility of ML). 11. Safeguards Question: Does the paper describe safeguards that have been put in place for responsible release of data or models that have a high risk for misuse (e.g., pre-trained language models, image generators, or scraped datasets)? Answer: [N/A] Justification: The paper poses no such risks. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper poses no such risks. • Released models that have a high risk for misuse or dual-use should be released with necessary safeguards to allow for controlled use of the model, for example by requiring that users adhere to usage guidelines or restrictions to access the model or implementing safety filters. • Datasets that have been scraped from the Internet could pose safety risks. The authors should describe how they avoided releasing unsafe images. • We recognize that providing effective safeguards is challenging, and many papers do not require this, but we encourage authors to take this into account and make a best faith effort. 12. Licenses for existing assets Question: Are the creators or original owners of assets (e.g., code, data, models), used in the paper, properly credited and are the license and terms of use explicitly mentioned and properly respected? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The paper properly credits all creators and original owners of assets used, and the licenses and terms of use are explicitly mentioned and respected. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not use existing assets. • The authors should cite the original paper that produced the code package or dataset. • The authors should state which version of the asset is used and, if possible, include a URL. • The name of the license (e.g., CC-BY 4.0) should be included for each asset. • For scraped data from a particular source (e.g., website), the copyright and terms of service of that source should be provided. • If assets are released, the license, copyright information, and terms of use in the package should be provided. For popular datasets, paperswithcode.com/datasets has curated licenses for some datasets. Their licensing guide can help determine the license of a dataset. • For existing datasets that are re-packaged, both the original license and the license of the derived asset (if it has changed) should be provided. • If this information is not available online, the authors are encouraged to reach out to the asset’s creators. 13. New assets Question: Are new assets introduced in the paper well documented and is the documentation provided alongside the assets? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The paper provides detailed documentation for all new assets introduced, including datasets, code, and models. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not release new assets. • Researchers should communicate the details of the dataset/code/model as part of their submissions via structured templates. This includes details about training, license, limitations, etc. • The paper should discuss whether and how consent was obtained from people whose asset is used. • At submission time, remember to anonymize your assets (if applicable). You can either create an anonymized URL or include an anonymized zip file. 14. Crowdsourcing and research with human subjects Question: For crowdsourcing experiments and research with human subjects, does the paper include the full text of instructions given to participants and screenshots, if applicable, as well as details about compensation (if any)? Answer: [N/A] Justification: The paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects. • Including this information in the supplemental material is fine, but if the main contribution of the paper involves human subjects, then as much detail as possible should be included in the main paper. • According to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics, workers involved in data collection, curation, or other labor should be paid at least the minimum wage in the country of the data collector. 15. Institutional review board (IRB) approvals or equivalent for research with human subjects Question: Does the paper describe potential risks incurred by study participants, whether such risks were disclosed to the subjects, and whether Institutional Review Board (IRB) approvals (or an equivalent approval/review based on the requirements of your country or institution) were obtained? Answer: [N/A] Justification: The paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects. • Depending on the country in which research is conducted, IRB approval (or equivalent) may be required for any human subjects research. If you obtained IRB approval, you should clearly state this in the paper. • We recognize that the procedures for this may vary significantly between institutions and locations, and we expect authors to adhere to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics and the guidelines for their institution. • For initial submissions, do not include any information that would break anonymity (if applicable), such as the institution conducting the review. 16. Declaration of LLM usage Question: Does the paper describe the usage of LLMs if it is an important, original, or non-standard component of the core methods in this research? Note that if the LLM is used only for writing, editing, or formatting purposes and does not impact the core methodology, scientific rigor, or originality of the research, declaration is not required. Answer: [N/A] Justification: The paper does not use LLMs as an important, original, or non-standard component. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the core method development in this research does not involve LLMs as any important, original, or non-standard components. • Please refer to our LLM policy in the NeurIPS handbook for what should or should not be described.

Affiliation: State Key Laboratory of Internet of Things for Smart City, University of Macau Abstract As AI-assisted image editing becomes increasingly prevalent, Text-Centric Image Forgery Localization (TFL) is essential for protecting trust in financial and legal records. However, we observe that existing TFL detectors predominantly rely on Full-Parameter Fine-Tuning (FPFT) and fail to generalize to unseen forgery types because FPFT can induce low-rank feature collapse and overfit training artifacts. Meanwhile, prior detectors capture diverse forgery traces with a single unified representation, making subtle traces entangled and difficult to learn. To address these challenges, we propose RiSE , a Residual Subspace Expert model that preserves pre-trained priors by freezing principal SVD components and adapting only the residual subspaces with a ViT-only segmentor to avoid feature collapse. RiSE introduces forgery-aware residual experts, where each expert is trained independently on a training subset with a particular forgery type, and we show that cross-domain localization performance improves consistently as more experts are added. At inference, we introduce Latent Perturbation Confidence (LPC), which selects the most confident expert by analytically computing the latent-perturbed output. LPC enables efficient confidence estimation with a single forward pass, avoiding repeated forward passes on perturbed samples and improving expert selection. By training on synthetic forgery data, RiSE with 1 expert outperforms prior methods on real-world forgery images by 20.4% while reducing training steps by 10 × 10\times . Scaling the number of experts to 9 yields a 35.8% gain. RiSE remains effective with DCT feature, even when the majority of the parameters is frozen with RGB-only pretraining. Code: https://github.com/KahimWong/RiSE . 1 Introduction Text-Centric Image Forgery Localization (TFL) aims to identify manipulated regions in scanned or captured text-centric images. This problem is increasingly important because modern AI-assisted editing tools allow ordinary users to alter document and scene-text images with little expertise ( Wong et al., 2025b ; Wong et al., 2025a ; Wong et al., 2026b ) , threatening trust in images used for financial verification, legal review, and identity authentication. Although recent TFL methods have improved accuracy by combining RGB, frequency ( Qu et al., 2023 ) , and multi-scale cues ( Dong et al., 2024 ) , their performance still drops sharply under cross-domain evaluation, where unseen forgery patterns and acquisition artifacts differ from the training distribution ( Du et al., 2025 ; Gushchin and others, 2026 ) . We argue that this failure is not merely a data scarcity issue. Unlike semantic segmentation, TFL depends on weak, non-semantic forensic traces whose statistics vary sharply across editing pipelines, recompression settings, and capture conditions. As a result, many existing TFL detectors ( Qu et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Wong et al., 2025c ) rely on Full-Parameter Fine-Tuning (FPFT) and end up specializing to the limited forgery patterns seen during training. Their penultimate features become highly low-rank, as shown in Fig. 1 , indicating representation collapse that harms cross-domain generalization. This observation points to a different formulation of TFL: the central challenge is to control where task-specific adaptation happens. Recent work on residual subspace adaptation ( Yan et al., 2025 ) shows that transferable priors from Vision Foundation Models (VFMs), typically built on the Vision Transformer ( Dosovitskiy et al., 2021 ) (ViT) architecture (e.g., CLIP ( Radford et al., 2021 ) , DINOv2 ( Oquab et al., 2024 ) , and DINOv3 ( Siméoni et al., 2025 ) ), can be preserved by freezing the dominant SVD components of ViT linear layers and fine-tuning only residual subspaces. This prior-preserving adaptation avoids representation collapse and improves performance in AI-generated image detection ( Yan et al., 2025 ) . However, bringing this idea to TFL requires more than inserting residual adaptation into an off-the-shelf segmentor. In TFL, the task-specific decoders and fusion modules can become a second adaptation pathway, allowing the model to memorize dataset-specific compression, synthesis, or capture artifacts outside the pre-trained backbone. At the same time, learning all forgery types in a single shared residual space entangles heterogeneous traces, causing subtle manipulation cues to be overwhelmed by dominant but less transferable patterns. This leads to two questions: (1) Can TFL be reformulated as a prior-preserving localization problem, with minimal trainable modules beyond the ViT so that adaptation remains constrained and transferable? (2) Can the limited trainable capacity be expertized, so that different residual subspaces specialize to complementary forgery cues and generalize better under domain shift? To answer these questions, we propose RiSE , a R es i dual S ubspace E xpert model for TFL built on a ViT-only segmenter. We instantiate RiSE on EoMT ( Kerssies et al., 2025 ) , which turns a ViT into a segmenter using only query embeddings and a lightweight mask module, thereby minimizing additional adaptation pathways beyond the backbone. On top of this architecture, RiSE divides the training set into non-overlapping subsets with a particular forgery type and trains one residual expert on each subset independently. All experts share the dominant principal subspaces of the VFM backbone, while each expert learns only a tiny residual subspace tailored to a more homogeneous forgery regime. We show that this offline image-level routing is more stable than learnable routing ( Shazeer et al., 2017 ) , and that scaling the number of experts consistently improves cross-domain performance as shown in Fig. 2 while parameter growth remains sublinear because the principal components are shared among experts. To select the final prediction among experts, we further propose Latent Perturbation Confidence (LPC), which addresses the limitation that existing confidence metrics ( Hendrycks and Gimpel, 2017 ; Borges et al., 2024 ) often become unreliable when forged regions are small. LPC estimates the expected latent-perturbed output analytically and favors experts whose forged predictions remain stable under perturbations. As a result, LPC enables single-pass confidence estimation, avoiding repeated forward passes on perturbed samples and improving expert selection for more accurate localization. Trained on DocTamper ( Qu et al., 2023 ) synthetic forgery data, a single RiSE expert generalizes effectively to real-world forgery images, achieving a substantial 20.4% performance improvement while reducing training steps by 10 × 10\times compared with existing TFL methods. Scaling to 9 experts further boosts the performance gain to 35.8%. Our contributions are fourfold: • We identify uncontrolled task-specific adaptation as a key cause of poor cross-domain TFL, show that FPFT induces low-rank feature collapse, and reformulate TFL as a prior-preserving localization problem with a ViT-only residual adaptation architecture. • We introduce residual subspace experts for TFL, each optimized on a training subset with a specific forgery type, so that different residual subspaces specialize to complementary forgery cues and improve cross-domain localization as more experts are added while keeping parameter growth sublinear. • We develop a plug-and-play confidence estimator, LPC, that analytically computes expected latent-perturbed outputs to measure expert confidence effectively and efficiently. • Extensive experiments demonstrate that RiSE consistently improves cross-domain localization performance by 35.8% across 4 test sets. 2 Related Work General image forgery localization increasingly focuses on robust trace modeling across manipulation types. Representative methods such as MVSS-Net ( Chen et al., 2021 ) and PSCC-Net ( Liu et al., 2022 ) use multi-scale cues, CAT-Net ( Kwon et al., 2022 ) exploits JPEG DCT statistics, and later work including IFOSN ( Wu et al., 2022 ) , TruFor ( Guillaro et al., 2023 ) , FOCAL ( Wu et al., 2025 ) , and Mesorch ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) improves generalization through modeling Online Social Networks (OSN) transmission, noise fingerprint, contrastive feature, and designing CNN–Transformer structure. Nevertheless, general image forgery detectors often struggle on text-centric images because forged regions can blend into the uniform backgrounds and structured text layouts. Text-centric image forgery localization has progressed from early benchmarking to DCT-aware and robustness-oriented detectors ( Wong et al., 2026a ) . DTD ( Qu et al., 2023 ) introduced the DocTamper benchmarking and showed that DCT perception with multi-scale decoding can effectively localize tampered regions. FFDN ( Chen et al., 2024 ) and ADCD-Net ( Wong et al., 2025c ) further improved localization through RGB–DCT fusion, with ADCD-Net explicitly addressing DCT misalignment and text-background disparity. TIFDM ( Dong et al., 2024 ) strengthens trace enhancement and multi-scale aggregation under degradations, CAFTB ( Song et al., 2025 ) combines spatial and noise-domain cues with cross-attention fusion, and DITL 2 \text{DITL}^{2} improves performance through learning from both general and text-centric image forgeries ( Li et al., 2025 ) . However, most existing TFL detectors rely on FPFT, which overfits training forgery patterns and induces low-rank feature collapse, harming cross-domain generalization. In contrast, RiSE preserves transferable priors via residual subspace adaptation and uses forgery-aware residual experts for stronger specialization and generalization. 3 Method Figure 1 : Effective-rank comparison of penultimate features across 8 datasets. Prior TFL detectors (DTD, FFDN, and ADCD-Net) concentrate most representation variance in a very small number of directions, while RiSE-1 (one expert RiSE) maintains a substantially higher effective rank, indicating a less collapsed and more expressive representation. (a) (b) Figure 2 : More residual experts improve (a) training optimization and (b) cross-domain localization. RiSE- x x denotes the RiSE with x x residual experts. In (b), RiSE-3 and RiSE-9 report oracle expert selection, i.e., the upper bound obtained by choosing the best expert with the ground-truth mask. Motivation. Recent TFL methods such as DTD ( Qu et al., 2023 ) , FFDN ( Chen et al., 2024 ) , and ADCD-Net ( Wong et al., 2025c ) rely on FPFT. As shown in Fig. 1 , these models produce strongly low-rank features, overfit to training forgery traces, and perform worse on cross-domain data ( Du et al., 2025 ) . Motivated by residual subspace adaptation ( Yan et al., 2025 ) , we use a ViT-only segmenter ( Kerssies et al., 2025 ) to keep the architecture minimal and preserve transferable VFM priors. RiSE maintains an effective rank that is roughly 4.7 − 37.3 × 4.7-37.3\times higher than these prior methods across the 8 datasets, suggesting that residual subspace adaptation better preserves transferable knowledge and avoids feature collapse. The effective rank computation is detailed in Appendix C . Our second motivation is the scaling behavior of residual experts. For TFL, we argue that modeling diverse forgery patterns and image context with a single space could lead to entangled and noisy representations ( Tu et al., 2026 ) . Therefore, we propose to split the training data into subsets with a particular forgery type and train a residual expert on each subset independently. Adding residual experts consistently improves training optimization in Fig. 2 (a), as well as enhancing cross-domain localization in Fig. 2 (b). For RiSE with multiple experts, we report the oracle performance, which assumes access to the ground-truth mask to choose the best expert for each sample and therefore serves as an upper bound on expert selection. Overview. RiSE is a residual subspace expert model for TFL built on a ViT-only segmenter. Let the training set be 𝒟 = { ( 𝐗 i , 𝐘 i , d i ) } i = 1 N \mathcal{D}=\{(\mathbf{X}_{i},\mathbf{Y}_{i},d_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N} , where 𝐗 i ∈ ℝ 3 × H × W \mathbf{X}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times H\times W} is a forgery image, 𝐘 i ∈ { 0 , 1 } H × W \mathbf{Y}_{i}\in\{0,1\}^{H\times W} is the ground-truth mask, and d i ∈ { 1 , … , N e } d_{i}\in\{1,\dots,N_{e}\} is the expert-assignment label of the i i -th sample. As illustrated in Fig. 3 (a), RiSE partitions the training set by the Cartesian product of N s N_{s} forgery synthesis types and N c N_{c} feature-cluster indices, yielding N e = N s × N c N_{e}=N_{s}\times N_{c} non-overlapping sub-training sets 𝒟 = ⋃ j = 1 N e 𝒟 j \mathcal{D}=\bigcup_{j=1}^{N_{e}}\mathcal{D}_{j} . Details of the expert assignment are provided in Appendix B . Definition 1 (RiSE Expert) .
